+**Lemma 11.3 (Dense sublevel localization retaining the moment deficit).** Fix $L>0$. For all sufficiently large $a$, uniformly over $0<\delta\le L/a$, every actual dense law with $H\le H_d$ satisfies
+
+$$
+\sqrt V\le\frac{24\delta}{r\mu^3},\qquad
+0\le\Delta\le72\delta^2\mu^{-6},\qquad
+\max_i|c_i|=O_L(r\delta).
+\tag{11.6}
+$$
+
+In particular $y_i=\mu+O_L(\delta/r)$ for every label. These are consequences for this sublevel and are not extra assumptions on the law domain.
+
+**Proof.** Set $R_i=c_i+b$, as in Lemma 3.1. Its pointwise nonnegative residual is
+
+$$
+(1-I_i)(2r+1)(r-K)+I_i(s-K)(s-K-1).
+$$
+
+Consequently
+
+$$
+R_i\ge0,\qquad
+\sum_iR_i=S_0+\Delta,\qquad S_0=6r\delta.
+\tag{11.7}
+$$
+
+The sum identity follows from $\sum_i c_i=\mathbb E K^3-r^2q$ and $Z-r^2q+sb=6r\delta$. With $f(y)=r^2/y-b/y^2$, (8.6)–(8.8) give, for all sufficiently large $a$ in the stated window,
+
+$$
+H=\sum_i f(y_i)+\sum_i\frac{R_i}{y_i^2},\qquad
+\sum_i f(y_i)\ge sf(\mu)+\frac{r^2}{2}V,
+\qquad sf(\mu)+\frac{S_0}{\mu^2}=H_d.
+$$
+
+Indeed $\mu\ge1/2$ and $b/(r^2\mu)\le1/12$ eventually, and density is exactly the other hypothesis needed in (8.7). Put $M=\max_i y_i$. Since $M\le1$, the inverse-square tangent inequality yields
+
+$$
+\begin{aligned}
+\sum_i\frac{R_i}{y_i^2}
+&\ge\frac{S_0+\Delta}{M^2}\\
+&\ge\frac{S_0}{\mu^2}
+ -\frac{2S_0}{\mu^3}(M-\mu)+\Delta\\
+&\ge\frac{S_0}{\mu^2}
+ -\frac{2S_0}{\mu^3}\sqrt V+\Delta.
+\end{aligned}
+$$
+
+Thus
+
+$$
+H-H_d\ge\Delta+\frac{r^2}{2}V
+ -12r\delta\mu^{-3}\sqrt V.
+\tag{11.8}
+$$
+
+Under $H\le H_d$, nonnegativity of $\Delta$ first gives the bound for $\sqrt V$ in (11.6). Maximizing $12r\delta\mu^{-3}u-r^2u^2/2$ over $u\ge0$ gives the displayed bound for $\Delta$. Finally (11.7) implies
+$|c_i|\le b+S_0+\Delta=O_L(r\delta)$, since $\delta/r$ is uniformly bounded and tends to zero. ∎
+

+**Theorem 8.2 (The surplus between the square-root and transition scales).** For every integer sequence with
+
+$$
+\frac{h}{\sqrt a}\longrightarrow\infty,
+\qquad \frac{h}{a^{3/2}}\longrightarrow0,
+$$
+
+one has
+
+$$
+\frac{M(a,h)-B_0(a)}{a^{3/2}h}\longrightarrow4.
+\tag{8.2}
+$$
+
+**Proof.** Theorem 2.1 is a lower bound for every original law, so
+
+$$
+M(a,h)-B_0(a)
+\ge\beta_a(h+1)-2a^2-a.
+$$
+
+Here $\beta_a/a^{3/2}\to4$, $h\to\infty$ and $\sqrt a/h\to0$. Division by $a^{3/2}h$ gives the lower limit at least $4$.
+
+For a matching upper bound choose
+
+$$
+j=\left\lceil\frac{h}{2\sqrt a}\right\rceil.
+$$
+
+Then $j\to\infty$, $j/a\to0$, $j/h\to0$ and $j\sqrt a/h\to1/2$. In particular $1\le j\le h$ eventually. Use the exact law of Theorem 3.1 at this varying integer $j$, rather than its fixed-$j$ asymptotic formula. Its feasibility for each such integer can also be read directly: with $m=a+j$, $n=h+1-j$ and $p=j/(m-1)$, the core mass $1-p=(a-1)/(m-1)$ and the $n$ singleton masses $p/n$ sum to one, their actual marginals are respectively $1-p>0$ and $p/n>0$, and
+
+$$
+\mathbb E K=(1-p)m+p=m-p(m-1)=a.
+$$
+
+Thus, for every $1\le j\le h$, not just fixed $j$, the unrestricted infimum is at most the exact energy
+
+$$
+H_j(a,h)=\frac{(a+j)^3(a+j-1)}{a-1}
+       +\frac{(h+1-j)^2(a+j-1)}j.
+\tag{8.3}
+$$
+
+For $1\le j\le a/2$, expansion of its first term has a uniform remainder:
+
+$$
+\begin{aligned}
+\frac{(a+j)^3(a+j-1)}{a-1}
+ &=a^3+4a^2j+R_{a,j},\\
+R_{a,j}
+ &=\frac{a^2j+3a(2a-1)j^2+(4a-1)j^3+j^4}{a-1}
+ =O(aj^2+aj).
+\end{aligned}
+\tag{8.4}
+$$
+
+The constant is absolute, as follows by bounding $j/a\le1/2$ in the displayed expression. Our choice of $j$ eventually lies in this range. The contribution of $4a^2j$ divided by $a^{3/2}h$ tends to $2$, while the remainder divided by the same quantity is
+
+$$
+O\!\left(\frac{h}{a^{3/2}}+\frac1a\right)=o(1).
+$$
+
+For the other term of (8.3), the exact normalized expression is
+
+$$
+\frac{(h+1-j)^2(a+j-1)}{j a^{3/2}h}
+=\left(\frac{h+1-j}{h}\right)^2
+ \frac{a+j-1}{a}\,\frac{h}{j\sqrt a}
+\longrightarrow2.
+$$
+
+Finally $(B_0(a)-a^3)/(a^{3/2}h)=(2a^2+a)/(a^{3/2}h)\to0$. This actual law gives the upper limit at most $4$, proving (8.2). No law attaining $M$ was used. ∎

+The classical identities used as intermediate steps are
+
+$$
+r(p,q)=(e_p-e_q)^{\mathsf T}L^+(e_p-e_q),\qquad
+R(c)=n\operatorname{tr}L^+=n\sum_{k=2}^n\lambda_k^{-1}.
+\tag{1.3}
+$$
+
+Here $L^+$ is inverse to $L$ on $\mathbf1^\perp$ and zero on constants.
+The primary supplier for (1.3) is Ghosh–Boyd–Saberi,
+[*Minimizing Effective Resistance of a Graph*, SIAM Review 50(1), 37–66,
+DOI:10.1137/050645452](https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/papers/pdf/eff_res.pdf),
+§2.4, equation (8), and §2.5, equations (13)–(15): their $G$, $g$ and

+
+$$
+x^{\mathsf T}Lx=\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(x_{u_i}-x_{v_j})^2.
+\tag{1.4}
+$$
